prompt: A colleague smooths the cutoff *after* an exponential mapping (the cutoff is 20 Hz multiplied by 1,000 to the power of the knob value, then a one-pole smoother runs on the cutoff in hertz). Users say turning the cutoff knob down feels sluggish, while turning it up feels snappy, wherever the knob is. Why, and what is the fix?

options.text: Exponential maps are always sluggish; use linear
options.explanation: A linear map would make the knob unmusical. The problem is where the smoothing happens, not the map.

options.text: The one-pole filter is unstable at high frequencies
options.explanation: With 0 < a < 1 a one-pole smoother is stable at any value, and instability would not produce a direction-dependent feel.

options.text: The ADC is slower at high voltages
options.explanation: ADC conversion time does not depend on the input voltage like this, and the complaint depends on direction, not position.

options.text: A one-pole in hertz closes a fixed fraction of the *hertz* gap, which is lopsided in pitch: rises cover most of their musical distance early, falls lag behind. Smooth the 0–1 value (or log-frequency) first, then map
options.explanation: Correct. Pitch is heard as a ratio. Hertz-domain smoothing reaches about 79% of the pitch distance of a ×5.6 rise after one time constant, but only about 42% of a ×5.6 fall. Smoothing before the map gives 63% both ways.

workedExample:
Take a quarter-turn move between 3,557 Hz and 20,000 Hz (a ×5.6 ratio) and look after one time constant, when a hertz-domain smoother has covered 63% of the gap in hertz. Musical (pitch) progress is measured by ratios, so use logarithms:

```formula
f_1 = f_a + 0.632 × (f_b − f_a)
p = ln(f_1 / f_a) / ln(f_b / f_a)
f_up = 3557 Hz + 0.632 × 16443 Hz
f_up ≈ 13950 Hz, p_up ≈ 0.79
f_down = 20000 Hz − 0.632 × 16443 Hz
f_down ≈ 9608 Hz, p_down ≈ 0.42
where
f_a: the starting cutoff, in hertz (Hz)
f_b: the target cutoff, in hertz (Hz)
f_1: the cutoff after one time constant
p: pitch progress, the fraction of the musical distance covered (0 to 1)
ln: the natural logarithm, which turns ratios into distances
f_up: f_1 for the upward move, 3,557 Hz to 20,000 Hz
p_up: p for the upward move
f_down: f_1 for the downward move, 20,000 Hz to 3,557 Hz
p_down: p for the downward move
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the same 63% in hertz is 79% of the way in pitch going up but only 42% coming down.
```

Repeat it at the bottom (20 ↔ 112 Hz) and you get the same 79% and 42%: hertz smoothing depends only on the ratio and direction, not on where you are. Smooth the 0–1 knob value, then map, and both directions reach 63% of the musical distance.
